scenes.title: A map, not a pile of protocols

cues.text: A useful validation master plan helps a new team member understand how
qualification and validation are governed.
In European Union GMP Annex 15, the programme may be defined in a
VMP or equivalent document.
This is not a requirement to give every site the same template.
Our worked plan is a teaching structure.
The applicable quality system determines the authorized document structure
and approval responsibilities.
For our small oral-liquid project, the plan links the mixing vessel,
transfer equipment, utilities and supporting procedures.
A scope table records the system identifier, intended use,
responsible owner and current evidence status.
An entry called complete without a report reference is difficult to challenge.
An explicit status such as design review pending tells the team what still
needs to happen.
A date in a schedule is not proof of qualification.
The programme plan explains the approach and oversight.
A protocol states how a particular verification will be performed and judged.
A report evaluates what actually happened.
The diagram presents these as connected documents rather than
interchangeable files.
For example, the plan may require risk-informed testing;
the protocol specifies a particular mixing test;
the report evaluates the observed results and any deviations.
Now suppose the project adds a second product with different cleaning needs.
Reusing the original plan unchanged may conceal a new scope.
Compare the new use with the approved assumptions, identify the affected
systems, and route updates through the quality system.
In the activity, prepare a short programme outline with owners,
document references and review triggers.
A useful plan should help people act, not merely describe intentions.
